display_title: Official Review of Paper438 by Reviewer bcvt

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work studies generalization and optimization aspects of deep neural networks from the prism of convex optimization, more specifically by treating the loss as a PL function on the domain of weights near initialization (and also near optimality for polynomially wide DNNs). The authors first collected various known results, showing that bounds on and training and generalization accuracy can be made, given that the DNN+loss is a PL function and, importantly, given the smoothness parameters associated with the specific PL function. 

The domain around initialization for which a DNN is PL and these smoothness coefficients depend on architecture details and width. The authors proceed in bounding these coefficients using a notion of Well-Conditioned layer which they introduce. This combined with other results on neural tangent kernels in the overparameterized results, allows them to bound the smoothness parameters based on a layer by layer analysis as opposed to one relying on the overall kernel or the Hessian of the DNN. Finally, empirical results are shown, on deep fully-connected DNNs, showing that despite being well away from the polynomially-over-parametrized region, PL type reasoning still partially holds in the sense that 
1. The training loss estimate at epoch n+1 given an estimate of the PL smoothness parameters at n, fits well the experimental curves within a factor of $2$ throughout raining, and fits very well after roughly 10% training was done. 
2. The lowest gram matrix eigenvalues of the top layer remains constant throughout training and the bound derived from it is highly non-tight.
content.main_review:
The theoretical part of the work, while interesting, seems somewhat incremental. Its main contribution seems to be the notion WC and the layer-by-layer estimates they derive for the conditioning (referred to above as steepness parameters above) all of which seem to be relevant in the polynomially over-parameterized region, where various competing approaches exist. This is especially true after half a decade of NTK related results and given that it's quite clear that real-world DNNs operate well away from the regime where NTK predictions hold. 

Turning to the experimental side of this work, its purpose is to show that the theory holds away from NTK like regimes. However, the most compelling evidence given, as far as I could tell, that the PL approach generalizes well to finite width is the estimation of the difference in loss between two adjacent epochs. Given that the bound is calculated at epoch $n$ and predicts the loss at $n+1$ following a minor change in weights doesn't feel like a very stringent test to me. In addition, it is done only for a single fully-connected DNNs whereas the main phenomenological difference between kernel methods and DNNs appear for CNNs.
content.summary_of_the_review: The theoretical side is not sufficiently distinct. The experiments are not compelling enough to show applicability to real-world DNNs.

content.comment:
> The theoretical part of the work, while interesting, seems somewhat incremental. Its main contribution seems to be the notion WC and the layer-by-layer estimates they derive for the conditioning (referred to above as steepness parameters above) all of which seem to be relevant in the polynomially over-parameterized region, where various competing approaches exist. This is especially true after half a decade of NTK related results and given that it's quite clear that real-world DNNs operate well away from the regime where NTK predictions hold.

Especially since it is clear that real DNN operate away from NTK regime, but there are currently no theories that predict in which way real DNN behave, we think that it is a good intermediate step to ask which techniques or reasonment do continue to hold, and which other do not. We also perform experiments to help validate the proposed theories and to have at least a starting point for the investigation

> Turning to the experimental side of this work, its purpose is to show that the theory holds away from NTK like regimes.

The purpose of the experiments is instead to investigate which parts of the theory hold and which other do not. We think that in this case, where both theories and detailed experiments on real DNN are scarce, negative results are relevant and tell which parts of the theories need to be improved.

> Given that the bound is calculated at epoch $n$ and predicts the loss at $n+1$ following a minor change in weights doesn't feel like a very stringent test to me. In addition, it is done only for a single fully-connected DNNs whereas the main phenomenological difference between kernel methods and DNNs appear for CNNs.

When considered cumulatively over many epochs we obtain the (newly added) plots in Figure 9 and 10 (Appendix F), which in fact show that the prediction degrades with the number of epochs and is better behaved for Tanh networks than ReLU networks.

Moreover the experiments have been conducted only on fully-connected networks because of memory limits in the computation of eigenvalues of linear layers. We emphasize that some differences between infinite-width networks and real DNN have been uncovered also by the performed experiments, such as the need for renormalization after each layer to allow conditioning to continue improving (Figure 1).

content.title: Reply to authors

I appreciate the author's reply. 

While there is no handle at the moment on finite width real-world DNN there are various works studying finite width effects via perturbative corrections or by modifying the associated Gaussian Processes  (see for instance https://journals.aps.org/prx/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevX.11.031059), or considering toy models with few layers (https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.05355). 

In light of this and following my impression regarding the power and generalizability of the current "intermediate steps" taken in the work, I leave my score as is.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper provides the convergence and generalization analyses of gradient descent based on a variant of PL-condition. The main contribution of the study is to propose a Well-Conditioned (WC) function which to verify the constant of PL-condition.
content.main_review:
[Strengths]

This study aims to develop a general theory based on PL-condition for neural networks. This sort of analysis is important to give theoretical guarantees for various network architectures rather than the limited class of networks.

[Weaknesses]

This study builds upon well-known results such as convergence analysis under PL-condition and smoothness, and generalization analysis using algorithmic stability. Hence, the contribution is essentially the verification of assumptions of these results and is rather incremental. 

This paper is difficult to understand because of the ambiguity of notations and lack of detailed explanation about definitions and examples.

- Notations of the derivative are unclear. It is better to provide the definition or comment for $D f_{x_i}$, $\nabla_i f$ on the Banach space. I guess $\nabla_i f(x)$ and $D f_{x_i}$ represent the same derivative from the proof Lemma 1. Is $\nabla_i f(x)$ an element in Banach space that corresponds to Frechet derivative $D f_{x_i}$? In that case, the notation $D f_{x_i}$ is ambiguous because the point $x$ where the derivative is taken is not described.
- Notation for the point $x$ is also confusing. For instance, $x_i$ seems to be $i$-th element of $x$ and $x_k$ in (2) is a $k$-th iterate.
- The correspondence between the notations for general theory and the examples of practical neural networks is not provided. Hence, I'm not sure how to apply this analysis to specific neural networks. The lack of concrete examples obscures the importance of the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: Basically, I think this line of research is important, but the paper is not ready for publication because of ambiguity.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper438 by Reviewer 5idT

content.title: Reply
content.comment:
> The notation is very hard to follow. It is quite challenging to aggregate the main contribution of the paper from the current version.

We apologize if our notation made understanding of the paper contribution difficult. We have now updated the notation following also the Reviewer's comments, and we hope that this now will allow the Reviewer to deepen their reading and understanding of the work. Please consider the changes in red in the new submission.

> First, I am not sure what is the main result? Lemma 5/6? Composition of WC is WC?

The main technical result of the paper consist in the introduction of WC functions as a tool to prove PLness of certain objectives (Section 4). On the other hand the main contribution is the proposal of a theory for actually-sized mildly overparameterized neural networks, for which no theoretical work is currently available to our knowledge, and the extensive experimental evidence provided, whose focus is the highlight of which parts of neural network training are explained by the available theories and which other are not.
Of course if the reviewer feels we have missed some highly relevant work in this sense, we will be very interested in being directed to such work.

> Second, what new insights we can get from the current theory, in additional to the existing works of overparameterized network (NTK) etc. ?

Existing works on NTKs qualitatively describe only infinite-width networks or extremely overparameterized networks (i.e. where the number of neurons in each layer is cubic in the number of examples) and thus fail to provide explanations for the networks used in practice (consider for example the sized of the networks winning the ImageNet contest).
There are no theories concerning the latter networks, and our paper is a first attempt, that must be judged as such.
Notable insights in our opinion include the surprising accuracy of the prediction of training loss decrease via PL optimization theory, the validation of the conditioning theory for finite-width networks (and its dependence on normalization after each layer as can be seen in figure 1), and the unexplained observation that the lowest eigenvalues of the H matrix do not degrade as much during training (Figure 2).

> Lemma5. There are too many to unpack in eq (3) while many of the notations are not clearly defined! E.g., what is $D_{g_{f(x)}}$?

We apologize again for the lack of clarify of the notation. In that part $Dg_{f(x)}$ is the Frechét differential of $g$ taken in the point $f(x)$. We have clarified our notation in the new paper revision, please read the changes in red.

> The notation of the equation in Lemma 6 $h(,_{ij} x_{ij})$ seems un-standard to me.

We find the notation extremely useful, even though unstandard. Consider how cleanly the dependencies on PL parameters can be expressed in Lemma 6.

> Lemma 7. Why $f$ is analytic? When $\sigma$ is the Relu, $f$ is not analytic.  In Agarwal, there are some normalization assumptions on $\sigma$, do you need them here? $H^{L+1} =\hat \sigma(H^L)$ is not correct, unless some assumptions are met! E.g., the network is infinite-wide!

Indeed, when $\sigma$ is the ReLU function, $\hat\sigma$ as defined in "Bounding the eigenvalue" paragraph is analytic, as can be seen in Daniely et al. (2016), p. 14, paragraph "The normalized ReLU activation".

Normalization assumptions on $\sigma$ are needed later in the experimental part (as highlighted in the paragraph "Experimental section") but not for the derivation of such theory.

We also remind the reviewer that Section 5 only exposes available theoretical arguments that are correctly justified only in infinite-width networks, and the paper sets out to verify how much they hold in finite-width networks experimentally.

> Is there a typo in the equation in Def 6, where the upper index $k$ should be change to some letter with range between 1 and k?

We are grateful to the reviewer for the typo corrections.

> For pre-image of a function can be simply written as $T^{-1}y$, which is quite standard. Using $S(T, y)$ makes the notation more convoluted.

The notation $S(T, y)$ is extremely useful not to be confused with assuming $T$ is invertible and in better expressing some proofs (consider Lemma 11). We are very open to reconsider this choice if the reviewer feels that there is a clearer unambiguous notation.

> As mentioned above, the notations of the paper are confusing that I don't think the paper is ready for publication.

Many thanks for pointing this out. We have updated the paper and clearly defined notation before its usage.

> In Eq (4), $\alpha$ is a matrix, which norm do you refer to $||\alpha||_2$, operator norm , Frobenus norm?

Rather than being a matrix, we view $\alpha$ as a vector of coefficients in this part, so that its 2-norm is standard euclidean norm which corresponds to Frobenius norm when $\alpha$ is seen as a matrix.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper comes up with a novel theoretical framework that trys to explain the optimization and generalization of (overparameterized) deep neural networks. This paper comes up with the concept of well-conditioned (WC) neural networks, and defines the WC coefficients $\lambda_i$ to be the norm of the inverse of the Jacobian. This paper then connects WC to Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) functions. PL is a function class where gradient descent could achieve linear convergence. This paper shows that PL and WC properties are well-preserved under function composition, thus connecting WC to optimization and generalization in deep neural networks. Based on existing theoretical results about PL functions, this paper designs and demonstrates experiments on real-world deep neural networks.
content.main_review:
#### Strengths
1. This paper provides a novel theoretical framework for deep learning theory that connects certain data-dependent properties (WC coefficents) to  properties related to optimization and generalization (PL). 
2. This paper conducts experiments to justify their theory. The mixing theoretical-empirical approach is rare in deep learning theory, but is crucial, and should be encouraged. Remarkably, certain experiments match well with the theory.

#### Weakness
1. The WC coefficients are closely related to the neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory. I guess the difference may be that the WC coefficients are data-dependent and do not assume gaussian initialization? I would suggest the authors draw more connections between them.
2. Fig 2. looks too good to be true. The loss convergence bound (e.g., Lemma 1) is a very rough estimate based on e.g., assuming that $L_i$ are the same everywhere, so this should leave a gap between predict loss curve and real loss curve, and thus I would only expect that they are equal up to bounded constant, i.e., $\frac{\mathrm{predicted\ loss}}{\mathrm{real\ loss}} \in [c_1, c_2]$ for some $0 < c_1 < c_2 < \infty$. However, the plot seems to suggest that $c_1 = c_2 = 1$. Can the authors explain why this should be the case?
3. The generalization bound in Lemma 3 is defined with respect to the sample size $n$, so I do not understand why Fig. 3 uses epoch as the horizontal axis, and I think it should be better using $n$ instead. Besides, instead of plotting the predicted generalization bound, I would suggest the authors to plot the ratio, i.e., $\frac{\mathrm{predicted\ generalization}}{\mathrm{real\ generalization}}$, and show if it is bounded. 
4. Though the authors focus on the overparameterized neural networks, I think there is no difficulties to extend, at least the empirical part, of this paper, to finite-width neural networks, so I would suggest the authors to also show experimental results for finite-width neural networks. It would be good for the community to know whether the results extend to the finite-width case.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think this paper has decent theoretical and empirical novelty, but I have some concerns, so I would currently recommend weak accept.

content.comment:
> The WC coefficients are closely related to the neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory. I guess the difference may be that the WC coefficients are data-dependent and do not assume gaussian initialization? I would suggest the authors draw more connections between them

We would like to ask the help of the reviewer in clarifying what they refer to when they mention the connection between WC coefficients and NTK theory. The paper focus is on networks far away from the NTK regime, and in complete honesty, the authors fail to see such a connection.

>  Fig 2. looks too good to be true. The loss convergence bound (e.g., Lemma 1) is a very rough estimate based on e.g., assuming that $L_i$ are the same everywhere, so this should leave a gap between predict loss curve and real loss curve, and thus I would only expect that they are equal up to bounded constant, i.e., $\frac{\mathrm{predicted\ loss}}{\mathrm{real\ loss}} \in [c_1, c_2]$ for some $0 < c_1 < c_2 < \infty$. However, the plot seems to suggest that $c_1 = c_2 = 1$. Can the authors explain why this should be the case?

The plot reports only the ratio between the real and predicted loss at epoch n+1 based on the loss at epoch n, thus only reports the relative misprediction at one epoch. When considered cumulatively over many epochs we obtain the (newly added) plots in Figure 9 and 10 (Appendix F), which in fact show that the prediction degrades with the number of epochs and is better behaved for Tanh networks than ReLU networks.

> The generalization bound in Lemma 3 is defined with respect to the sample size $n$, so I do not understand why Fig. 3 uses epoch as the horizontal axis, and I think it should be better using $n$ instead. Besides, instead of plotting the predicted generalization bound, I would suggest the authors to plot the ratio, i.e., $\frac{\mathrm{predicted\ generalization}}{\mathrm{real\ generalization}}$, and show if it is bounded.

While the dependence on $n$ is standard, the plot in Figure 3 highlights the role of increased optimization in the decrease of generalization bounds, a fact that is hinted at by Lemma 4, but whose experimental confirmation was needed because of the possibility for the lipschitz coefficient $G$ to also increase during training.
The suggested plot is obviously bounded since the real generalization is always greater than zero. We will add the plot in the appendix to show also how these two quantities are related.

> Though the authors focus on the overparameterized neural networks, I think there is no difficulties to extend, at least the empirical part, of this paper, to finite-width neural networks, so I would suggest the authors to also show experimental results for finite-width neural networks. It would be good for the community to know whether the results extend to the finite-width case.

Indeed our results already do focus on finite-width networks, especially in the experimental part. The aim of the paper is to highlight differences and similarities between what is predicted by theories on very wide neural networks vs what happens in real-world cases of mildly overparameterized networks (i.e. where the number of neurons in each layer are a constant factor larger than the number of examples).

content.title: General comment to Reviewer
content.comment:
We would like to address here some concerns common to many reviewers to clarify the main novelties of the work and to differentiate our work from NTK research; we also prepared a review of our paper that clearly defines the used notation, and we hope this will allow reviewers concerned about the notation to hopefully deepen their analysis of the paper and provide feedback relative to its contributions. Performed changes are marked in red in the resubmission to ease tracking of changes.  Let us first state that while our work is completely based on the study of finite-width networks, and particularly mildly overparameterized networks, i.e. where the number of neurons in each layers is larger than a small constant factor from the number of examples, and thus considers vastly different networks than the NTK theory.
As mentioned by reviewer #bcvt it is clear that finite width networks do not behave as infinite-width ones under the NTK, but as far as we know there are no theoretical studies providing theories for actual-sized finite-width networks, because of the difficulty in providing complete theories for those networks; our paper is a first step toward understanding what are the exact problems of studying finite-width networks and adopts a novel mixed theoretical-experimental approach, where the performed experiments try to inform the theory of such networks. Of course if the reviewer feels we have missed some highly relevant work in this sense, we will be very interested in being directed to such work (with our apologies for having missed it).  Novelties of our work thus are: (1) the introduction of the set of WC function, a useful and general tool to prove PLness of certain classes of functions (2) the proposal of a theory for real-world-sized neural networks; the theory considers various aspects of neural networks (conditioning, training, and generalization) and experimentally verified predictions on those. We highlight that the theory is based on known methods which are however used and combined in a novel way, and provides a substantial amount of experimental evidence, which is directed at informing enhancements of the theory.

content.title: Similarity to prior works
content.comment:
Dear authors,

Recently I noticed your submission to this ICLR. You talked about convergence under PL condition, and introduced the well-condition concept for over-parameterized neural networks. It seems like there are a lot of overlap with our previous works [1][2], that establish optimization theory for over-parameterized NN. 

>In our works, we showed that over-parameterized neural networks, as functions of its parameters, are uniformly conditioned (similar to the well condition in your submission). 

>Based on that, we show that the loss function for over-parameterized NNs satisfy the PL condition.

> Based on PL condition we further show the convergence of gradient descent methods.

I would like to see your opinions on these similarities.

[1] C Liu, et al, Loss landscapes and optimization in over-parameterized non-linear systems and neural networks, arXiv:2003.00307

[2] C Liu, et al. On the linearity of large non-linear models: when and why the tangent kernel is constant. NeurIPS 2020.

replying_to: Replying to Similarity to prior works

content.title: Reply
content.comment:
We agree there are a remarkable number of similarities, as well as some important differences in the approach and results.
Similarities are based on the usage of a variation of the PL condition (PL* or local PLness in the paper of Liu et al., and a modified PL that accounts for differences in the PL constant of each layer in ours), and in the derivation of a convergence theory for such condition that parallels standard theory on the PL condition. Later an analysis of the conditioning of over-parameterized networks shows that such functions do satisfy the variation of the PL condition, and thus can be optimized.

The first difference between the works is the matrix on which the conditioning is computed: in Liu et al. the “tangent kernel matrix” $DF(x) DF(x)^T$ is considered, for $F: \mathbb{R}^m \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^n$, while in our work we consider $H_x = F_x F_x^T$ where $F$ is a matrix computed by the inner feature of the data passing through a network layer.
This difference also translates in the different approaches considered to bound the displacement of the minimum kernel matrix eigenvalues: Hessian-based in Liu et al. and matrix-distance-based in our work, and also reflects in the given theorems on convergence.

Another difference is the methodological approach: Lee et al. focus on obtaining clear theorems and a theory that is both general and applicable to wide neural networks with asymptotical bounds. On the other hand our work focuses on providing general intuitions of the methods that have been used to analyze wide neural networks, with a special focus on quantitative estimates for real-world networks. We identify key lemmas and quantities that other work depends on (e.g. Du et al. 2019 for what concerns convergence guarantees of first-order methods), and we prepare multiple experimental settings on FCNs to collect data that can help identifying which of those lemmas and quantities do describe actual behaviour of real-world networks.
Thus our work is more exploratory in nature and tries to consider multiple facets of neural network theory (convergence, conditioning, generalization), while it does not focus too much on providing an organic theory that is able to explain everything on a special classes of neural networks, but rather tries to highlight which of the existing theories serves well the explanatory purpose.

Other minor differences are: (1) Liu et al. mainly consider the mean squared error loss, and later provide some theorems for generically PL* loss functions, while our work also works for generic PL loss functions (thus including all strongly convex functions) via Lemma 5. (2) We find that the notion of WC function is more general than the considered hessian approach in Liu et al. and could possibly simplify some of the provided proofs. Particularly concerning the note in Remark 3 that “Even if the original system had a small Hessian norm, there is no such guarantee for the transformed system.”, we think that the notion of WC function could possibly give a more invariant way to frame the results.

We find the paper of Liu et al. extremely interesting and relevant for our research and in the interest of a stimulating discussion we would like to ask the authors a few questions:
1. How much difficult would it be to derive quantitative bounds for e.g. Theorem 4, which expresses the dependency $m = \tilde\Omega(n)$ but does not provide clear constants, in order to possibly test empirically the predictions of the two theories?
2. Do you think it is possible to refine the current theory to explain real-world-occurring overparameterized neural networks where e.g. $m = 2n$ or do you think that novel techniques have to be found to address such networks?
